news.headline: Kiwi engineers learn from Venezuela's devastating earthquakes
news.body: Last month, four New Zealand engineers flew to Venezuela to help in the aftermath of the devastating double quakes, which hit the western and central parts of the country in June, leaving more than 6000 people dead. Nearly 200 buildings collapsed in the quakes while more than 16-thousand structures were deemed unsafe. For the Kiwi engineers, it was a chance to learn about what New Zealand could do better, when it comes to earthquake resilience. University of Canterbury civil and environmental engineering Professor Santiago Pujol, director of the earthquake research centre, QuakeCore spoke to Ingrid Hipkiss.

logs.summary:
A powerful earthquake, initially measured at magnitude 7.1 (later revised to 6.8), struck Kumamoto Prefecture in southern Japan on July 28, 2026, at 4:27 p.m. local time. The quake caused the partial collapse of the Aeon Mall in Kashima, trapping many people and leaving an unknown number dead, while injuring at least 50 others and causing widespread damage including fires, power outages, and damage to historic Kumamoto Castle.
A 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck southern Japan's Kyushu island near Kumamoto on July 28, 2026, causing a shopping mall to partially collapse with multiple people trapped and feared dead. The quake knocked out power to thousands of homes, ruptured roads, triggered a temporary tsunami advisory, and left dozens injured, with up to 30 mall employees missing after an explosion.

The river, which flows through 10 countries, has receded to unprecedented lows, exposing rocks and old shipwrecks. In Budapest, the Danube was measured at just 23 centimeters, breaking previous records. River cruise ships are docking upriver, and sightseeing cruises have been canceled. Rocky Mount, Virginia issued a voluntary water conservation request due to ongoing drought conditions, with the town receiving only about half its normal rainfall. In North Dakota, dry weather has caused hay shortages, with drought-damaged cereal crops down to 50% of normal, prompting producers to plan late-season alfalfa management. Separately, forecasters warn that the 2026-27 El Niño is strengthening into a very strong event, increasing the risk of heat and erratic rainfall.
Recent reports show drought persisting across several regions: central Minnesota's drought held steady while statewide conditions eased slightly, and eastern Idaho farmers are expecting lower potato yields due to drought and heat. Alabama's drought has been increasing, especially in southern and western areas, while St. Thomas has deteriorated into exceptional drought even as Puerto Rico saw slight improvement. Forecasts warn of a potentially unprecedented El Niño in 2026/27 that could bring below-normal rainfall to South Africa, and drought combined with the Black Sea grain crisis is raising global food security concerns, while El Niño-driven drought in Papua New Guinea has forced school sports cancellations.
